questions.stem: According to Tajfel and Turner's social identity theory, what is the order of the three processes?
options: Social categorisation, social comparison, social identification
Social categorisation, social identification, social comparison
Social comparison, social categorisation, social identification
Social identification, social comparison, social categorisation
questions.explanation: People first sort themselves and others into groups (categorisation), then take on the identity of their group (identification), and finally compare their group with others (comparison).

questions.stem: On her first day at a new school, Kira notices students sorting each other into 'sporty kids', 'gamers' and 'arty kids'. Which process of social identity theory is this?
options: Social responsibility
Social categorisation
Social identification
Social comparison
questions.explanation: Sorting people into groups based on shared features is social categorisation, the first process in social identity theory. Identification comes later, when a person adopts a group's identity.

questions.stem: After joining the school choir, Ben starts wearing the choir badge, adopts its traditions and feels proud when it performs well. Which process does this show?
options: Social influence
Social identification
Social categorisation
Social comparison
questions.explanation: Taking on the identity and norms of the group, and linking one's self-esteem to it, is social identification. Social comparison would involve comparing the choir with other groups.

questions.stem: Students at one school regularly say their school is friendlier and smarter than the school down the road. Which process of social identity theory does this show?
options: Social identification
Mutual interdependence
Social comparison
Social categorisation
questions.explanation: Comparing the in-group favourably with an out-group is social comparison. Tajfel and Turner proposed that this boosts the self-esteem of the in-group's members.

questions.stem: According to social identity theory, why do people compare their own group favourably with other groups?
options: To maintain or increase their self-esteem
To compete for scarce physical resources
To reduce cognitive dissonance about past actions
To obey the instructions of a group leader
questions.explanation: Because people's self-esteem is partly tied to their group memberships, seeing the in-group as better than out-groups raises self-esteem. Competition for scarce resources is a different explanation of intergroup conflict.

questions.stem: Students are split into two groups by a coin toss. Without ever meeting, they share points between the groups and give more to their own group. Which theory best explains this?
options: The contact hypothesis
Social identity theory
The just-world phenomenon
Kelman's social influence theory
questions.explanation: Even trivial, randomly assigned groups lead people to favour their in-group, as social identity theory predicts, because categorisation alone is enough to trigger in-group favouritism. There is no competition for real resources and no contact between the groups.

questions.stem: Which is a limitation of social identity theory?
options: It does not fully explain why some people show much more in-group bias
It cannot explain why people would favour their own group over others at all
It has never been tested in any experimental research
It proposes that all prejudice is caused only by a person's personality traits
questions.explanation: Social identity theory explains in-group favouritism in general but says less about why individuals and groups differ in how strongly they show it. It has been tested in many experiments, including studies with trivially formed groups.

questions.stem: A stereotype is:
options: a goal that two groups can only reach by working together
a generalised belief about the characteristics of members of a group
a negative feeling towards a person because of their group
unfair treatment of a person because of the group they belong to
questions.explanation: A stereotype is a generalised belief about the members of a group, which can be positive or negative. A negative feeling is prejudice, and unfair treatment is discrimination.

questions.stem: Stereotypes are described as a form of social categorisation because they:
options: assign characteristics to people based on the group they are placed in
always lead directly to unfair treatment of out-group members
are learned only from direct experience with each individual
are made up of only the behavioural component of an attitude
questions.explanation: Once people are categorised into a group, stereotypes attach the group's assumed traits to them. Stereotypes do not always lead to discrimination, and they are often learned indirectly rather than from personal experience.

questions.stem: What is the main function of stereotypes?
options: They act as mental shortcuts that make judging people quicker
They give an accurate picture of each individual within a group
They prevent people from sorting others into social groups at all
They ensure that people treat members of all groups equally
questions.explanation: Stereotypes simplify the social world, letting people make quick judgements without much mental effort. The cost is that they ignore individual differences and can be inaccurate.

questions.stem: What is a key disadvantage of relying on stereotypes?
options: They take a great deal of mental effort to use in everyday life
They can only ever be positive, so they hide real group differences
They make it impossible for people to belong to any group
They ignore individual differences and can lead to inaccurate judgements
questions.explanation: Because a stereotype applies the same traits to every member of a group, it overlooks individual differences and can produce wrong judgements. Stereotypes save mental effort rather than costing it, and they can be positive or negative.

questions.stem: Prejudice is best defined as:
options: a generalised belief that all members of a group are the same
a negative attitude towards people because of their group membership
unfair behaviour towards people because of their group membership
a rule that applies equally to everyone but disadvantages one group
questions.explanation: Prejudice is an attitude, usually negative, held towards people because of the group they belong to. Unfair behaviour towards them is discrimination.

questions.stem: Discrimination is best defined as:
options: holding a negative attitude towards members of a particular group
a generalised belief about the members of a particular group
the tendency to see one's own group as better than others
treating people unfairly because of their membership of a group
questions.explanation: Discrimination is behaviour: treating people unfairly because of their group membership. Holding a negative attitude without acting on it is prejudice.

questions.stem: Which statement about the relationship between prejudice and discrimination is correct?
options: Prejudice and discrimination are the same thing, so one cannot exist without the other
Discrimination always comes first, and prejudice develops only after a person has discriminated
Discrimination is an attitude, while prejudice is a type of behaviour towards a group
A person can hold prejudice without acting on it, so it need not lead to discrimination
questions.explanation: Prejudice is an attitude and discrimination is behaviour, so a person may hold a prejudice but not act on it, for example because of laws or social norms. Discrimination is the behaviour, not the attitude.

questions.stem: A manager believes older workers are slow to learn, and rejects every job applicant over 50. Which statement is correct?
options: The belief shows prejudice, and rejecting the applicants is discrimination
The belief is discrimination, and rejecting the applicants shows prejudice
Both the belief and the rejections are examples of discrimination only
Both the belief and the rejections are examples of prejudice only
questions.explanation: The manager's negative view of older workers is a prejudiced attitude, and turning them away is discriminatory behaviour, here based on age. Prejudice is the attitude and discrimination is the action.

questions.stem: Direct discrimination occurs when:
options: a person holds a negative attitude but never acts on it
two groups compete for the same limited resources
a person is treated worse than others because of a characteristic such as race
a rule that applies equally to everyone unfairly disadvantages one particular group
questions.explanation: Direct discrimination is openly treating someone worse because of a characteristic such as race, gender, age or disability. A rule that applies to everyone but disadvantages a group is indirect discrimination.

questions.stem: Which is an example of indirect discrimination?
options: A club whose only entrance is a flight of stairs, excluding people who use wheelchairs
A landlord who refuses to rent a flat to a family because of their ethnic background
A shop owner who tells young people they are not welcome to enter the shop
An employer who refuses to promote a worker simply because she is a woman
questions.explanation: The stairs apply to everyone but disadvantage people with a mobility disability, which is indirect discrimination. Refusing someone because of their ethnicity, age or gender is direct discrimination.

questions.stem: A company advertises a job requiring 'ten years of unbroken full-time work'. The rule applies to all applicants but excludes many women who have taken parental leave, and it is not needed for the job. This is:
options: prejudice without discrimination
the group-serving bias
indirect discrimination
direct discrimination
questions.explanation: A requirement that applies to everyone, is not reasonable for the job, and disproportionately disadvantages one group is indirect discrimination. Direct discrimination would be rejecting women openly because they are women.

questions.stem: An employer refuses to interview anyone who has been treated for depression, believing they will be unreliable. This is an example of:
options: indirect discrimination based on age
a superordinate goal set by the employer
the self-serving bias in hiring decisions
prejudice and discrimination based on mental illness
questions.explanation: The employer holds a negative belief about people with depression (prejudice) and acts on it by excluding them (direct discrimination based on mental illness). Nothing here concerns age or a shared goal.

questions.stem: The just-world phenomenon is the tendency to believe that:
options: one's own group deserves more than other groups
people's behaviour is caused mainly by the situation
the world is fair, so people get what they deserve
everyone has equal access to the same resources
questions.explanation: The just-world phenomenon is the belief that the world is fair and people get what they deserve. It can lead people to blame victims for their own misfortune, which feeds prejudice.

questions.stem: "People who are homeless must have made bad choices; anyone who works hard ends up with a home." Which cause of prejudice does this statement best show?
options: Equal-status contact
The just-world phenomenon
Intergroup competition
Mutual interdependence
questions.explanation: Assuming people deserve their misfortune reflects the just-world phenomenon, which leads to blaming victims. Intergroup competition involves groups competing for limited resources.

questions.stem: Two neighbouring towns compete for a single new sports centre, and hostility between their residents grows. Which cause of prejudice does this show?
options: Social responsibility
Superordinate goals
Intergroup competition
The just-world phenomenon
questions.explanation: Competition between groups for a limited resource increases hostility and prejudice between them. A superordinate goal is the opposite: a shared goal that reduces conflict.

questions.stem: A child who often hears his parents and friends mock a particular ethnic group begins to hold the same negative views. Which cause of prejudice does this show?
options: Equal-status contact
Social influence
Intergroup competition
The just-world phenomenon
questions.explanation: Prejudice can be learned from family, peers and the media, and people adopt it to fit in with the views of those around them. This is social influence as a cause of prejudice.

questions.stem: How does social categorisation contribute to prejudice?
options: Treating each person as a unique individual makes stereotyping more likely
Sorting people into groups removes any need to compare one group with another
Dividing people into 'us' and 'them' encourages favouring the in-group over out-groups
Placing people in groups always leads to open and violent conflict between the groups
questions.explanation: Once people are sorted into an in-group and out-groups, they tend to favour 'us' and see 'them' as all alike, which can lead to prejudice. Categorisation does not always lead to open conflict.

questions.stem: The contact hypothesis proposes that prejudice can be reduced by:
options: keeping the groups apart until tensions settle
telling each group that the other is to blame
increasing competition between the two groups
contact between groups under the right conditions
questions.explanation: The contact hypothesis states that bringing groups together can reduce prejudice, but only under certain conditions, such as equal status and working towards shared goals. Mere contact alone is often not enough.

questions.stem: A superordinate goal is:
options: a goal that each member of a group pursues privately on their own
a goal that both groups want but can only reach by working together
a goal that one group can only reach by defeating the other group
a goal set by a leader that group members must obey without question
questions.explanation: A superordinate goal is a shared goal that no group can achieve alone, so it requires cooperation. A goal one group reaches by defeating another creates competition, which increases prejudice.

questions.stem: In a 'jigsaw' classroom, each student in a mixed group holds one part of the information needed, so the group can only succeed if everyone contributes. Which condition for reducing prejudice does this create?
options: Intergroup competition
Social categorisation
The just-world phenomenon
Mutual interdependence
questions.explanation: When group members must rely on one another to succeed, they are mutually interdependent, which encourages cooperation and reduces prejudice. Competition between groups would increase prejudice.

questions.stem: Why does the contact hypothesis require equal-status contact?
options: If both groups have equal status, they will compete much harder for the same resources
Equal status means the groups never need to work together
Equal status prevents members from identifying with their group
If one group has lower status in the contact, existing stereotypes may be reinforced
questions.explanation: When groups meet as equals, members can see each other as individuals, but unequal status can confirm existing stereotypes. Equal status is meant to encourage cooperation, not competition.

questions.stem: What was the aim of the Robbers Cave experiment (Sherif et al., 1954)?
options: To study whether bystanders help less when others are present
To study how competition creates intergroup conflict and how it can be reduced
To study whether people will obey orders from an authority figure to harm another person
To study whether people conform to a group's obviously wrong answers
questions.explanation: Sherif and his colleagues studied how competition between groups produces hostility and prejudice, and how that conflict could then be reduced. Obedience was Milgram's focus.

questions.stem: Who were the participants in the Robbers Cave experiment?
options: Mixed groups of adults recruited through a newspaper
Infants observed with their mothers in a playroom
About 22 boys aged around 11 or 12 at a summer camp
Male university students paid to take part in a laboratory
questions.explanation: The participants were about 22 boys of around 11 or 12 years old, who were taken to a summer camp in a state park in Oklahoma and divided into two groups. They were similar in background so that differences between them could not explain the conflict.

questions.stem: Which sequence describes the stages of the Robbers Cave experiment?
options: Integration, then in-group formation, then competition between the groups
In-group formation, then integration, then competition between the groups
In-group formation, then competition between the groups, then integration
Competition between the groups, then in-group formation, then integration
questions.explanation: First each group formed its own identity, then the groups competed in contests for prizes, and finally the researchers tried to reduce the conflict in the integration stage.

questions.stem: What happened during the competition stage of the Robbers Cave experiment?
options: Hostility grew, with name-calling, raids on each other's cabins and a flag being burned
The boys quickly formed friendships across the groups and agreed to share their prizes
The boys refused to compete any further and asked the researchers to end the contests
The losing group left the camp, so the study ended early
questions.explanation: Competing for prizes led to strong hostility between the two groups, including name-calling, cabin raids and flag burning. This supported the idea that competition for limited resources produces intergroup conflict.

questions.stem: Which finding about reducing conflict came from the Robbers Cave experiment?
options: Bringing the groups together for meals and films did not reduce hostility, but superordinate goals did
Bringing the groups together for meals and films ended hostility, so no other steps were needed
Hostility ended only when the researchers separated the groups for the rest of the camp
Superordinate goals increased hostility, because the groups argued about who should lead
questions.explanation: Simple contact, such as shared meals, did not reduce conflict and sometimes led to more fighting. Hostility fell when the groups worked together on superordinate goals, such as fixing the camp's water supply.

questions.stem: Which is a limitation of the Robbers Cave experiment relating to generalisability?
options: The boys were all of similar background, so the results may not apply to other groups
There were too many participants for the researchers to observe them closely
The study took place in a laboratory, so the boys' behaviour was unnatural and artificial
The boys were adults, so the results may not apply to children
questions.explanation: The sample was a small group of boys of similar age and background, so the findings may not generalise to girls, adults or other cultures. The study took place in a natural camp setting, not a laboratory.

questions.stem: Which ethical concern applies to the Robbers Cave experiment?
options: The boys were paid so much that their participation was not voluntary
The boys did not know they were in a study and were exposed to conflict and possible harm
The boys were given electric shocks whenever their group lost a contest
The boys' names and results were published without their parents' knowledge or consent
questions.explanation: The boys were not told they were being studied, and the researchers deliberately created hostility that could cause psychological harm. No electric shocks were involved.

questions.stem: What was the main contribution of the Robbers Cave experiment?
options: It showed that attitudes change when people act against them for only a small reward
It showed that people conform to a majority on an obvious perceptual task
It showed competition causes intergroup hostility and superordinate goals reduce it
It showed that people obey authority figures even when told to harm others
questions.explanation: The experiment showed that competition for limited resources can create prejudice and hostility between groups, and that working towards superordinate goals can reduce it. Obedience to authority was shown by Milgram.
